teaser: Four women, four kinds of weather, and the print set that put Mucha in Paris living rooms.
review_notes:
Image is a low-resolution composite of the four 1896 panels (Spring, Summer, Autumn, Winter) with warm, saturated color; spots point at large regions only. Identification as the 1896 series (not the 1897 or 1900 sets) is based on the compositions: Spring with a lyre and birds, Winter warming a bird.
Mucha's exclusive contract with the printer F. Champenois in 1896, with a regular monthly payment, and his move to a larger studio in rue du Val-de-Grâce that year.
Earlier poverty: his patron Count Khuen-Belasi ended his allowance around 1889; he lived above Madame Charlotte's crémerie in rue de la Grande-Chaumière.
Panels also issued in luxury printings on satin.
Spring's lyre made from a branch and her own hair: standard description, hard to verify at this image size.

lesson.text: In 1896 Alphonse Mucha could finally stop counting coins. Only a few years earlier the Czech illustrator had been living on lentils in a small room above a cheap Paris eatery, after the count who paid for his studies cut him off. Then a theater poster for Sarah Bernhardt made him famous almost overnight.

Fame brought a contract. The printer Champenois offered Mucha a steady monthly payment in exchange for the exclusive right to print his designs. Mucha moved into a big new studio. Champenois, for his part, wanted to sell as many sheets as possible.

So the two of them tried an idea: pictures with no product on them. No theater, no biscuits, no bicycle. Just a beautiful image on a tall sheet, cheap enough for a clerk or a shopkeeper to hang at home. They called these “decorative panels”, and The Seasons was the first set.
The panels were printed by color lithography, from flat stones inked one color at a time, and sold as a set of four. Buyers who wanted something fancier could get them printed on satin.
The subject was ancient. Painters had turned the seasons into people for centuries. Mucha's version gives each one a woman, a plant and a mood. Read them from left to right, like a year.

lesson.title: One year, four panels
lesson.text: Each panel has its own color of light. Notice how the women's poses change with the weather.

spots.title: Spring
spots.text: A blonde girl in a thin white dress stands under white blossom. She is the only one on her feet and half dancing. Her hands are busy with a green twig bent into a small harp.

spots.title: Summer
spots.text: A dark-haired woman crowned with red poppies sits on a bank, leaning on a vine, her bare feet hanging toward the water. The sky is hot blue. Nobody is doing anything.

spots.title: Autumn
spots.text: Wearing a wreath of chrysanthemums, she reaches for a bunch of dark grapes with one hand and holds a white bowl in the other. This is the season that works: harvest.

spots.title: Winter
spots.text: Wrapped from head to foot in a pale green cloak, she huddles by a bush loaded with snow. All the bare skin of the other three panels is gone.

lesson.text: Standing, lounging, harvesting, huddling: without a single written word, the four bodies tell you the temperature. That was the whole point of a picture meant to be understood from across a room.
Mucha's decorative panels turned the art print into something ordinary people could afford, and brought Art Nouveau from the street into the home.

Art Nouveau, the “new art” of the 1890s, loved lines borrowed from plants: stems, tendrils, hair that curls like smoke. Mucha drew a dark contour around every shape and filled it with soft flat color. Here the hair of Summer and Autumn twists into the vines until you cannot tell which is which.
Winter is the quietest panel, and the easiest to pass over. Yet it holds the one small act of kindness in the whole set.
Winter is not only keeping herself warm. Find what she is holding close to her mouth.

spots.title: A frozen bird
spots.text: She cups a small bird in her hands and breathes on it to warm it. Just below, on a branch, other little birds sit fluffed up against the cold, as if waiting their turn.

lesson.text: With that bird the series ends on tenderness and not on cold. And Spring, at the other end, has birds too, perched on her little harp. The year closes into a circle, ready to start again.
The set sold so well that Champenois asked Mucha for the same subject again. He designed a second Seasons in 1897 and a third in 1900, each with new poses.

spots.title: Spring's harp
spots.text: A bent green branch makes the frame of a tiny lyre, a small harp, and small birds sit on it. In the usual reading its strings are strands of her own hair.

spots.title: Poppies
spots.text: Big red poppies sit like a hat on Summer's dark hair. They flower in the hot months, and their red is the strongest note in the panel.

spots.title: Feet in the water
spots.text: Summer's bare feet dangle just above the surface of a pond, where tall reeds grow. The pose says heat better than any sun could.

spots.title: Chrysanthemums
spots.text: Autumn's crown is made of spiky pale chrysanthemums, the flower of late in the year, painted grey-blue against her red-brown hair.

spots.title: The grapes
spots.text: At the left edge of the panel her hand closes on a cluster of dark grapes. Vine leaves around her have begun to turn red.

spots.title: Snow on the branches
spots.text: Thick white caps of snow sit on every twig of the bush. Mucha draws them with the same curling outline he uses for flowers.

lesson.text: Mucha later grew tired of being the man of pretty posters and went home to paint the history of the Slavic peoples on enormous canvases. But it is these four tall sheets, made in the first year he had money in his pocket, that ended up on walls around the world.

quiz.question: What changed for Mucha in 1896?
options: He lost his patron and left Paris
He signed an exclusive contract with a printer for a steady income
quiz.explanation: The printer Champenois paid him regularly for the right to print his designs.

quiz.question: What made a “decorative panel” different from a poster?
options: It advertised nothing and was meant for the home
It was painted by hand in oil
It was always printed in black and white
quiz.explanation: The panels carried no product: they were affordable images to hang at home.

quiz.question: Which season is shown gathering grapes?
quiz.explanation: Autumn reaches for grapes and holds a bowl: the harvest season.

quiz.question: What is Winter doing with her hands?
quiz.explanation: She holds a bird close to her mouth and breathes on it.

quiz.question: How did the public respond to the 1896 set?
options: It sold so well that two more Seasons sets followed
quiz.explanation: Mucha designed new versions in 1897 and 1900.

facts.text: The Seasons was Mucha's first set of decorative panels.
facts.explanation: It launched the idea of affordable prints made only to decorate.

facts.text: Summer wears a crown of chrysanthemums.
facts.explanation: Summer wears red poppies, and the chrysanthemums belong to Autumn.

facts.text: In Winter, the woman shows as much bare skin as in the other panels.
facts.explanation: She is wrapped from head to foot in a pale green cloak.
